data.section: The Unreformed System and the 1832 Reform Act
data.sourcePassage:
Before the Reform Act of 1832, Britain's parliamentary system was very unequal. The right to vote was limited and varied from place to place. Many men could not vote because they did not own enough property. Women could not vote in parliamentary elections. Power was strongly connected to land, wealth and status.

The Industrial Revolution made these problems more obvious. New industrial towns such as Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds and Sheffield grew rapidly but had little or no direct representation in Parliament. Meanwhile, some old boroughs with very few voters still elected MPs. These were known as rotten boroughs. Some constituencies were controlled by wealthy landowners who could influence or select the MP — these were called pocket boroughs.

Demands for reform grew for several reasons. Industrialisation created new towns and a wealthier middle class. Ideas about rights and representation spread. Economic hardship created anger when Parliament seemed to ignore ordinary people. Campaigners organised reform societies, public meetings, petitions and newspapers to spread their ideas.

The Reform Act of 1832 removed many rotten boroughs, created parliamentary seats for some growing towns, and gave the vote to more middle-class men. It made the political system look less obviously corrupt. However, most working-class men still could not vote, and women were excluded entirely. The 1832 Act mattered because it showed that Parliament could be changed by pressure — but it was a turning point, not the finish line.

questions.question: What was a rotten borough?
options: A town that had been destroyed by fire or disease
A constituency with very few voters that still elected MPs
A borough that had lost its market trading rights
An area that refused to follow the law
questions.modelAnswer: A constituency with very few voters that still elected MPs to Parliament.

questions.question: Why did the Industrial Revolution make demands for parliamentary reform stronger?
options: New factories created more wealthy landowners who controlled Parliament
New industrial towns with large populations had little or no parliamentary representation
The Industrial Revolution ended the need for reform by making people wealthier
Parliament had already granted new towns their own MPs
questions.modelAnswer: New industrial towns such as Manchester and Birmingham grew rapidly but had little or no parliamentary representation, making the old system look increasingly unfair.

questions.question: What did the Reform Act of 1832 achieve?
options: It gave all men and some women the right to vote
It gave working-class men the vote for the first time
It removed many rotten boroughs and gave more middle-class men the vote
It established secret ballots to prevent bribery
questions.modelAnswer: The 1832 Reform Act removed many rotten boroughs, created seats for some growing towns, and gave more middle-class men the vote.

questions.question: The passage describes 1832 as 'a turning point, not the finish line'. What does this mean?
options: The 1832 Act was irreversible and could never be changed
The 1832 Act was a significant change but democracy was still incomplete, with many still excluded from voting
The 1832 Act was actually unsuccessful and changed nothing
After 1832, no further reform was ever needed
questions.modelAnswer: The 1832 Act was a significant change — it removed rotten boroughs and expanded the vote — but most working-class men and all women were still excluded. It opened the door to further reform but did not complete the process.

data.sourcePassage:
Chartism was one of the most important working-class political movements in nineteenth-century Britain. It began after many working-class people felt betrayed by the 1832 Reform Act. They had helped demand reform but gained no vote from it.

In 1838, Chartists published the People's Charter. It had six main demands: votes for all adult men, secret ballots, no property qualification for MPs, payment for MPs, equal electoral districts and annual Parliaments. At the time these demands seemed radical to many in Parliament. Today, all but one — annual Parliaments — have become part of British democracy.

Chartists used many methods: mass meetings, petitions with huge numbers of signatures, newspapers, local political organisation and peaceful protest. Some Chartists supported peaceful persuasion, known as moral force; others believed stronger action, known as physical force, might be needed if Parliament continued to ignore them.

Chartists presented major petitions to Parliament in 1839, 1842 and 1848. Each was rejected. This can make Chartism look like a failure, but that is too simple. Chartism kept working-class political rights in public debate, showed that ordinary people could organise nationally, spread ideas about democracy and helped train future political campaigners. It is a good example of a campaign with limited short-term success but major long-term significance.

questions.question: What was the People's Charter?
options: A petition signed by wealthy landowners defending the old voting system
A list of six political demands published by Chartists in 1838
A new constitution written by Parliament in 1842
A legal document granting women the right to vote
questions.modelAnswer: A list of six political demands published by Chartists in 1838, including votes for all adult men and secret ballots.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'moral force' and 'physical force' Chartism?
options: Moral force Chartists believed in violence; physical force Chartists believed in peaceful petitions
Moral force Chartists supported peaceful persuasion; physical force Chartists believed stronger action might be needed
Both terms mean the same thing in the context of Chartism
Moral force Chartists were middle-class; physical force Chartists were all rural workers
questions.modelAnswer: Moral force Chartists believed in peaceful campaigning and persuasion. Physical force Chartists believed stronger, more confrontational action might be needed if Parliament kept ignoring them.

questions.question: Why were the Chartist petitions of 1839, 1842 and 1848 significant even though Parliament rejected them?
options: They were not significant because they achieved nothing
Parliament actually agreed to some demands but kept this secret
They showed ordinary people could organise nationally and kept working-class political rights in public debate
They convinced Parliament to pass the 1867 Reform Act immediately
questions.modelAnswer: Although rejected, the petitions showed that ordinary people could organise on a national scale, kept democratic ideas in public debate, and influenced future political campaigns.

questions.question: The passage describes Chartism as having 'limited short-term success but major long-term significance'. How does the passage support this judgement?
options: Chartists won the vote for all men by 1848
Chartism immediately led to the Second Reform Act of 1867
Chartist petitions were rejected, but most Charter demands later became part of British democracy
Chartists successfully reformed the House of Lords in the 1840s
questions.modelAnswer: The petitions were rejected at the time, but five of the six Chartist demands eventually became part of British democracy, showing their long-term significance despite short-term failure.

data.sourcePassage:
Women faced many legal and social inequalities in the nineteenth century. They were excluded from voting in parliamentary elections, and many people argued that politics was a male sphere. Campaigners for women's suffrage argued this was unjust: women obeyed laws and paid taxes, so they should have a voice in making laws.

Suffragists campaigned for women's votes using peaceful and legal methods. The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, formed in 1897 and led by Millicent Fawcett, used petitions, public meetings, speeches, pamphlets and lobbying of MPs. Fawcett believed peaceful campaigning would prove women were responsible citizens.

The Women's Social and Political Union, founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst and others, used more militant methods. Its members were known as suffragettes and their slogan was 'Deeds not words'. Suffragettes interrupted political meetings, broke windows, went on hunger strike in prison and damaged property. The government responded with arrests and force-feeding. The 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill Health) Act, nicknamed the 'Cat and Mouse Act', allowed hunger-strikers to be released when weak and re-arrested later. Historians still debate whether militancy helped or harmed the campaign.

The First World War changed the political context. Many women contributed through war work, nursing and munitions production. The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave all men over 21 and some women over 30 the vote. Younger women and many poorer women were still excluded. The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote on the same terms as men from age 21, marking a major step towards equal political citizenship.

questions.question: What was the main difference between suffragists and suffragettes?
options: Suffragists wanted votes for women; suffragettes wanted votes for men
Suffragists used peaceful methods; suffragettes used more militant tactics
Suffragists were led by Emmeline Pankhurst; suffragettes were led by Millicent Fawcett
Suffragists were working-class; suffragettes were upper-class
questions.modelAnswer: Suffragists used peaceful and legal methods such as petitions and lobbying. Suffragettes used more militant tactics such as window-breaking and hunger strikes.

questions.question: What was the 'Cat and Mouse Act' of 1913?
options: A law banning suffragette meetings and marches
A law allowing hunger-striking prisoners to be released when weak and re-arrested later
A law giving some women over 30 the vote
A law giving the police greater powers to arrest protesters
questions.modelAnswer: The Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill Health) Act 1913 allowed the government to release hunger-striking prisoners when they were weak and then re-arrest them when they recovered.

questions.question: What did the Equal Franchise Act of 1928 achieve?
options: It gave all adults over 18 the right to vote
It gave women the vote on the same terms as men, from age 21
It gave women over 30 who met property requirements the vote
It abolished the House of Lords and created a fully elected Parliament
questions.modelAnswer: The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote on the same terms as men from age 21, removing the remaining inequalities from the 1918 Act.

questions.question: The passage says historians 'still debate whether militancy helped or harmed the campaign'. What are the two sides of this debate?
options: Some argue militancy showed women were unfit to vote; others argue women were never given the vote
Some argue militancy forced the issue into public debate; others argue it gave opponents a reason to reject women's suffrage
Some argue militancy immediately won the vote in 1913; others argue it delayed the 1928 Act
Some argue both suffragists and suffragettes used identical methods; others argue the methods were completely different
questions.modelAnswer: Supporters argued that militant tactics forced women's suffrage into public attention and showed that women could not be ignored. Critics argued that militancy provided opponents with an excuse to claim women were irresponsible and unfit for the vote.
